entities.summary: Coriscus of Scepsis was a Greek philosopher and thinker of the Hellenistic era, active in Scepsis during the 3rd century BCE. He was a prominent student of Aristotle and later became the head of the Academy of Plato, succeeding the famous philosopher. Coriscus was known for his treatises on logic, metaphysics, and the nature of the divine, which had a lasting impact on Western philosophy. His ideas on Stoicism and the nature of reality influenced prominent philosophers such as Zeno of Citium and Chrysippus. Coriscus was also a prolific writer, and his works were widely studied and debated in the ancient world. He was particularly known for his contributions to the field of logic, which laid the groundwork for later philosophers such as Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius. Coriscus' writings also explored the nature of the divine, which had significant implications for the development of religious thought in the ancient world. His ideas on metaphysics and the nature of reality have had a lasting impact on Western philosophy, influencing thinkers such as René Descartes and Immanuel Kant. Coriscus' legacy can be seen in the many philosophers who built upon his ideas, including the Stoics and the Epicureans. Coriscus' contributions to logic and metaphysics have had a lasting impact on the development of Western philosophy, shaping the way we think about reality and knowledge. His influence can be seen in many areas of philosophy, including epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics.
